newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians, Chechens urge restraint despite violence.
newsitem.headline: Russians, Chechens urge restraint despite violence.

text.p: Russian and Chechen separatist leaders said on Wednesday they were committed to peace talks despite fresh tensions in southern Russia aggravated by the murder of a senior local official.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, who has blamed Chechen rebels for a string of recent violent acts outside Chechnya, said after meeting President Boris Yeltsin that no extra troops would be sent to the areas bordering the breakaway region.

Yeltsin's senior aide, Boris Berezovsky, and Kremlin chief of staff Ivan Rybkin rushed to the Chechen capital of Grozny to meet separatist leaders in a clear attempt to keep up the political dialogue.
The situation around Chechnya, where 21 months of war between Moscow troops and rebels ended in a shaky truce in August, has deteriorated badly in the past week.
On Wednesday unidentified gunmen killed Khamzat Dzeitov, deputy interior minister of the ethnic republic of Ingushetia bordering Chechnya, and his driver.
Interfax news agency quoted Russian security sources as saying police had also found and disarmed two car bombs in Ingushetia's capital, Nazran.

A week ago a powerful bomb killed two people in the southern town of Armavir. Another two people were killed and 20 were wounded on Monday when a bomb badly damaged the railway station in the spa resort of Pyatigorsk.
Kulikov said on Tuesday police had detained two Chechen women fighters suspected of organising the Pyatigorsk blast.
Also on Tuesday, Russian police fought a brief pre-dawn skirmish with a group of what they said were 20 Chechen fighters just outside Chechnya, resulting in casualties on both sides.

Chechen officials resolutely rejected any connection to the violence and Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov suggested to Rybkin that a joint investigation committee be set up, Itar-Tass news agency said.

Alongside a war of words, Chechen and Russian officials expressed fears the violence would disrupt peace talks and urged restraint. "We have to come to terms at last," Tass quoted Maskhadov as saying. "We had enough of mutual accusations."

The August ceasefire halted fighting but did not resolve the main dispute -- whether the rebel region should remain part of Russia or become independent. They two sides are now involved in difficult negotiations over a long-term peace treaty.
Tass quoted Rybkin as saying before starting the talks that there were forces aiming at maintaining hostility around Chechnya.
"Many people in Chechnya and in Russia want to disrupt the fragile peace, but we shall block such attempts," Rybkin said without specifying who exactly he meant.
Kulikov said after meeting Yeltsin at the Black Sea resort of Sochi that police were taking steps to reinforce security in southern Russia but were not planning to send any fresh troops.
"There are no plans to build up troops in the area," he told Russian Public Television.

Kulikov, who appears to be sticking to a tougher line on Chechnya than other Russian officials, said that the Grozny authorities could not control the situation in their own region and had rejected Moscow's help.
"We have taken certain measures to prevent the infiltration of criminals from Chechnya," Kulikov said. "But this does not mean at all sealing off the border between Russia and Chechnya."
"What we want is a full control over it," he added.
